title: Set up USPS mail forwarding
detail: Set the start date to your move date. Verifying your identity online costs about $1–2. Forwarding lasts 12 months.

title: Plan your move-out
detail: Give your landlord your new address in writing and take photos at move-out so your deposit comes back.

title: Schedule shutoff of your current utilities
detail: Electric, gas, and water. Ask for a final meter reading on move-out day.

title: Cancel or transfer internet and return equipment
detail: Returning the router or modem late usually means a fee.

title: Set up utilities at the new place
detail: Ask the landlord or seller which utilities you need to set up in your own name.

title: Book internet install for move-in day
detail: Install dates fill up at the start of the month.

title: Renters insurance for the new address
detail: Most leases require proof before move-in.

title: Homeowners insurance for the new home
detail: Your lender will need proof before closing.

title: Book moving day and building time slots
detail: Reserve elevators, loading docks, or street parking at both places.

title: Move prescriptions to a pharmacy near your new home
detail: Fill anything you need before the move so nothing runs out in between.

title: Cancel local-only memberships
detail: Gym, parking, storage, and other local subscriptions. Check their notice periods.

title: Register to vote in your new state
detail: Deadlines are often a few weeks before an election.

title: Update your address with the IRS
detail: File Form 8822, or just use your new address on your next return.

title: Plan for part-year state tax returns
detail: Moving mid-year usually means a part-year return in both states. Keep your lease or closing papers as proof of the dates.

title: Update the state tax withheld from your pay
detail: Ask payroll to switch withholding to your new state as of your move date.

title: Update your health insurance
detail: Employer plans need your new address, and doctors in the new area may not be covered. Marketplace plans usually need a new plan in your new state. Moving lets you enroll outside open enrollment, usually within 60 days.

title: Get car insurance in your new state
detail: Most states require a policy from the new state before you can register the car there.

title: Title and register your car in your new state
detail: Check your new state's DMV for the deadline and any inspection needed first.

title: Get a driver's license in your new state
detail: Most states give new residents 30–90 days.

title: Banks and credit cards
detail: Also update the billing address saved in Apple Pay, Google Pay, and your browser's autofill.

title: Investment, retirement, and student loan accounts
detail: Tax forms are mailed in January, so update these before year-end.

title: Employer, clients, and anyone who sends you tax forms
detail: Anyone who sends you a W-2 or 1099 needs your new address before January.

title: Phone carrier
detail: Update the billing address and the emergency (911) address used for Wi-Fi calling.

title: Shopping and delivery apps
detail: Delete the old address so orders don't go there by mistake.

title: Doctors, dentist, and pharmacy records
detail: Update your address, or ask for records to be transferred if you're switching providers.

title: Stop catalogs and junk mail
detail: DMAchoice (small fee), or each store's mail preferences page.

title: Update your business address with the state where it's registered
detail: Ask an accountant whether you also need to register the business in your new state.

title: Update the business address with the IRS (Form 8822-B)
detail: This keeps IRS letters and notices going to the right place.

title: Business bank, payments, domain contact, and invoices
detail: Anything that shows a business address, including your website's footer.

title: Treat every forwarded letter as an account you missed
detail: Anything with a yellow USPS forwarding sticker still has your old address. Add it on the Accounts tab.

title: Follow up on your security deposit
detail: If it hasn't arrived within your old state's deadline, send the landlord a written request.

title: Check your credit report for the new address
detail: A couple of months after the move, once accounts have been updated.

title: Check that your mover is registered
detail: Interstate movers must have a USDOT number. Look them up in the FMCSA database, get a written estimate, and expect the 'Your Rights and Responsibilities When You Move' booklet.

title: Reserve your truck or moving container
detail: Month-end dates book up first. Check whether either street needs a parking permit for the truck.

title: Check your new state's rules for bringing plants
detail: Some states restrict plants, soil and firewood crossing the border.

title: Plan the sale of your old home
detail: Keep homeowners insurance until closing, and tell your insurer if the home will sit empty.

title: Set up your old home as a rental
detail: Switch to a landlord insurance policy, decide who handles repairs, and expect to file a nonresident return in the old state for the rental income.

title: Tell your insurer the old home will be empty
detail: Many policies limit coverage for homes left vacant for more than a month or two.

title: Check for a homestead or property tax break
detail: Many counties lower property taxes on your main home, but you usually have to apply.

title: Buying a car after the move
detail: Get your new state's license first if you can, and register the car there from the start.

title: Title and register your motorcycle, boat, trailer, or RV
detail: Boats are often registered with the state's wildlife or boating agency rather than the DMV.

title: Tell HR about your new state
detail: Do it before you move. Payroll taxes change, and some employers can't pay people in every state.

title: Use your new address on new-job paperwork
detail: Your W-4 and your new state's withholding form should both show it.

title: Update your address with clients and payment platforms
detail: Anyone who sends you a 1099, plus Stripe, PayPal, Upwork and similar. Check whether your new city or county requires a business license, and switch estimated tax payments to your new state.

title: Update your address with your school and financial aid
detail: In-state tuition usually requires living in the state for about 12 months first, with proof like a lease and a state ID.

title: Update your pension and retirement accounts
detail: Also check how your new state taxes retirement income, and update state tax withholding.

title: Report the move to your unemployment office
detail: Keep filing with the state that pays your benefits, and ask how job-search rules work from the new state.

title: Cancel SNAP in your old state and apply in the new one
detail: You can't get SNAP in two states at once. Report the move, ask for a closure letter, and apply right away. Approval can take weeks, so plan for a gap.

title: Transfer WIC to your new state
detail: Ask your current WIC office for a transfer card, then contact the new state WIC office.

title: Update your address with Social Security
detail: Federal payments continue after you update your address. SSI amounts can change if the new state pays a different supplement.

title: Update your address with the VA
detail: Also look up your new state’s veteran benefits, which can include tax breaks.

title: Check your new state's veteran benefits
detail: Many states offer tax breaks, license plates, or a veteran mark on your license.

title: Talk to your base legal office before changing your legal residence
detail: Service members and spouses can often keep their home state for taxes and car registration.

title: Close Medicaid in your old state and apply in the new one
detail: Medicaid doesn't transfer between states. Apply as soon as you arrive, and plan for a possible gap.

title: Update your address with Social Security for Medicare
detail: Medicare Advantage and drug plans are regional, so moving out of your plan area lets you pick a new one.

title: Check that the plan covers doctors in the new area
detail: Out-of-state coverage on a parent’s plan can be limited to emergencies.

title: Enroll the kids in their new school
detail: Ask the old school to send records. The new district will want proof of address, usually a lease or closing papers.

title: Get on childcare waitlists and find a pediatrician
detail: Waitlists can be months long, so start before the move.

title: Get vet records and license your pet in the new county
detail: Bring vaccine and rabies records, update microchip contact details, and check whether your new county or building needs a pet license.

title: Transfer your professional license
detail: Check your new state's licensing board. Some fields have multistate compacts, and others take weeks to approve, so start early.

title: Check your new state's firearm laws before you move
detail: Transport, storage, registration and permit rules vary. Some local rules are stricter than the state’s.

title: Have your will and power of attorney reviewed
detail: They usually stay valid, but a local lawyer can confirm they work under your new state’s law.

title: Make sure your old voter registration is canceled
detail: Registering in the new state usually handles this. If it asks for your previous address, fill it in.

title: Make sure everyone moving updates their own accounts
detail: Each adult needs their own USPS forwarding (unless you share a last name), license, and voter registration.
